Unit 12 - Instrumental Variables

Jim Flynn

November 2, 2026

The Canonical IV setup

  • D is the treatment we are interested in
  • A good IV (Z) has two properties:
    • \(cov(Z,D) \neq 0\) (first-stage)
    • \(cov(Z,\epsilon) = 0\) (exclusion restriction)

Why do we need an IV?

  • Omitted Variable Bias (ability)
  • Simultaneity (supply and demand)
  • Measurement error
  • General endogeneity

A good IV should feel weird

  • It should not immediately make sense when you describe it to someone
  • Need to be able to defend the exclusion restriction
    • This means that it shouldn’t logically make sense that Z affects Y
    • If it does, it must be through an effect on X
  • In metrics terms: The IV is irrelevant to the outcome except for its effect on the endogenous variable

Examples of IVs

Regulating cold meds \(\implies\) ??? \(\implies\) Foster care

Child’s birthday \(\implies\) ??? \(\implies\) Odds of getting flu

Age of menarche \(\implies\) ??? \(\implies\) Education

Sex of 1st 2 kids \(\implies\) ??? \(\implies\) Mom’s labor supply

Election year \(\implies\) ??? \(\implies\) Crime

Marathons \(\implies\) ??? \(\implies\) Odds of surviving cardiac arrest (non-runners)

What’s the point

  • We want to know the effect of X on Y, but this is endogenous
  • We need variation in X that is free of OVB and simultaneity
  • IV that strongly affects X but does not affect Y gives us what we need
  • This exogenous variation in X allows us to capture the effect of X on Y

Let’s walk through an example

  • You want to estimate:

\(Y_i = \alpha + \beta X_i + \gamma U_i + \epsilon_i\)

  • But U is unobserved, so you run:

\(Y_i = \alpha + \beta X_i + \eta_i\)

  • Where

\(\eta_i = \gamma U_i + \epsilon_i\)

  • We have an OVB problem where:

\(OVB = \gamma \frac{C(U,X)}{V(X)}\)

OVB gives us biased estimate

  • We want to estimate \(\beta\)
  • We clearly can’t do that in one step
  • What if we could estimate something that we know includes \(\beta\)
    • Then, if we know the other piece, we could back into an estimate of \(\beta\) by itself

Some definitions will help us

  • Structural Equation - this is the true equation that describes the world

    • May not be estimable

  • First stage - equation that shows the effect of Z on X

  • Reduced Form - This is where we will plug the first-stage into the structural equation

In our setting

  • Structural equation:

\(Y_i = \alpha + \beta X_i + \gamma U_i + \epsilon_i\)

  • First stage:

\(X_i = \delta_0 + \delta_1 Z_i + \rho_i\)

  • Reduced form:

\(Y_i = \alpha + \beta (\delta_0 + \delta_1 Z_i + \rho_i) + \gamma U_i + \epsilon_i\)

\(Y_i = \alpha + \beta \delta_0 + \underbrace{\beta \delta_1}_{\text{Our focus}} Z_i + \beta\rho_i + \gamma U_i + \epsilon_i\)

What is the reduced form coefficient?

\(\frac{Cov(Z,Y)}{Var(Z)} =\frac{Cov(Z, \underbrace{\alpha + \beta \delta_0}_{constants} + \beta \delta_1 Z_i + \underbrace{\beta\rho_i}_{constant} + \gamma U_i + \epsilon_i)}{Var(Z)}\)

\(\equiv \frac{Cov(Z, \beta \delta_1 Z_i + \underbrace{\gamma U_i + \epsilon_i}_{\text{0 by assumption}})}{Var(Z)}\)

\(\equiv \frac{Cov(Z, \beta \delta_1 Z_i)}{Var(Z)} = \beta \delta_1 \frac{Var(Z)}{Var(Z)} = \underbrace{\beta \delta_1}_{\text{This includes }\beta!}\)

We have \(\beta\), what is \(\delta_1\) again?

  • \(\delta_1\) is the coefficient on \(Z\) from the first stage, so:

\[\frac{\frac{Cov(Z,Y)}{Var(Z)}}{\frac{Cov(Z,X)}{Var(Z)}}= \frac{Cov(Z,Y)}{Cov(Z,X)}= \frac{\beta \delta_1}{\delta_1}= \beta\] This gives us an unbiased coefficient for \(\beta\)!

OK we can find \(\beta\), but how do we do this via regressions?

  • There are multiple ways
  • We will use a procedure called two-stage least squares
    • aka 2sls
  • Uses OLS and has simple, intuitive design

Two-Stage Least Squares

  • Step 1 - regress \(X\) (endogenous) on \(Z\) (instrument)
    • Take fitted values (\(\hat{X}\))
    • It’s worth pausing to think what these represent
  • Step 2 - regress \(\hat{X}\) on \(Y\) (outcome)
    • Adjust SE’s (R will do this for us)

Let’s set this up

Z <- rnorm(10000)
U <- rnorm(10000)
X <- rnorm(10000) + 1*Z + 2*U
Y <- rnorm(10000) + 3*X + 4*U
  • Z is our instrument
  • U is our omitted variable (ability)
  • X is our variable of interest
  • Y is our outcome

Run the OVB version

ovb <- lm(Y~X)
summary(ovb)$coefficients
##                Estimate Std. Error     t value  Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept) -0.01267391 0.02518056  -0.5033213 0.6147495
## X            4.30832183 0.01029026 418.6794147 0.0000000

We can fix this by controlling for U

ctrl <- lm(Y~X+U)
summary(ctrl)$coefficients
##                 Estimate  Std. Error     t value  Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept) -0.005599872 0.009985955  -0.5607748 0.5749636
## X            2.993624618 0.006993912 428.0329257 0.0000000
## U            3.998390510 0.017274381 231.4636093 0.0000000

Now we will manually calculate the IV version

first_stage <- lm(X~Z)
X_hat <- fitted.values(first_stage)

iv_manual <- lm(Y~X_hat)
summary(iv_manual)$coefficients
##                Estimate Std. Error    t value      Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept) -0.02213971  0.1039155 -0.2130551  8.312884e-01
## X_hat        3.02264689  0.1017588 29.7040276 6.905390e-186

We can also take the ratio of the covariances

cov_zy <- cov(Z,Y)
cov_zx <- cov(Z,X)

beta_iv <- cov_zy/cov_zx
beta_iv
## [1] 3.022647

Solution 1

Z <- rnorm(10000)
U <- rnorm(10000) + 3*Z
X <- rnorm(10000) + 1*Z + 2*U
Y <- rnorm(10000) + 3*X + 4*U

summary(ivreg(Y~X|Z))$coefficients[1:2,1:4]
##               Estimate  Std. Error     t value  Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept) 0.02246663 0.020716491    1.084481 0.2781779
## X           4.70976970 0.002908806 1619.141808 0.0000000

Solution 2

Z <- rnorm(10000)
U <- rnorm(10000)
X <- rnorm(10000) + 1*Z + 2*U
Y <- rnorm(10000) + 3*X + 4*U + 3*Z

summary(ivreg(Y~X|Z))$coefficients[1:2,1:4]
##               Estimate Std. Error     t value Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept) 0.01144851 0.03588218   0.3190582 0.749689
## X           5.93473181 0.03358785 176.6928241 0.000000

Are there any drawbacks?

  • Notice that we used only a subset of the variation in X
  • Because of this, standard errors got bigger
    • We lose precision with IV
    • Power becomes very important
    • Especially power in the first stage

Weak Instruments problem

  • What happens if the relationship between the IV and X is not that strong?
    • We will obviously lose precision
    • Our estimate will also become biased

Let OLS bias be:

\(Bias_{OLS} = E[\hat{\beta}_{OLS}-\beta] = \frac{Cov(\epsilon,X)}{Var(X)}\)

Bias returns to OLS bias as instrument gets weaker

\(E[\hat{\beta}_{2SLS}-\beta] = (Bias_{OLS}) \frac{1}{F+1}\)

Where F is the F-stat on Z from the first-stage regression

  • As \(F \to \infty\), \(\hat{\beta}_{2SLS} \to \beta\)
  • As \(F \to 0\), \(\hat{\beta}_{2SLS} \to \beta_{OLS}\)

What is an F-stat again?

  • F-stat of a single variable \(Z\) in a regression is:

\[\frac{SSR_{old}-SSR_{new}}{n-k}\]

  • Where
    • \(SSR_{old}\) is the SSR without including \(Z\)
    • \(SSR_{new}\) is the SSR including \(Z\)
    • \(k\) is the total number of independent variables
  • To get a large \(F\), \(Z\) needs to explain a lot of variation in X

What’s the difference between T and F?

  • When \(k=1\), \(T^2=F\)
    • \(T = \frac{\hat{\beta}}{SE_{\hat{\beta}}}\), \(F = \frac{SSR_{old}-SSR_{new}}{n-k}\)
  • The difference is that F is more flexible
  • Can test multiple variables/instruments
  • T can only test one

Class exercise

  • Write a simulation with 1000 regressions
  • X and Y uncorrelated
  • Save T and F from each round
  • Make a scatter plot of T and F
  • This is how you save F
library(car)
X <- rnorm(1000)
Y <- rnorm(1000)
lm1 <- lm(Y~X)
F <- linearHypothesis(lm1,"X=0")$F[2]
F
## [1] 0.4236014

Solution

df <- data.frame(matrix(ncol=2,nrow=1000))
colnames(df) <- c("T", "F")

for (i in 1:1000) {

X <- rnorm(1000)
Y <- rnorm(1000)

lm1 <- lm(Y~X)

T <- summary(lm1)$coefficients[2,3]
F <- linearHypothesis(lm1,"X=0")$F[2]

df[i,1] <- T
df[i,2] <- F
}

Solution scatterplot

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(df, aes(x=T,y=F)) + 
  geom_point()

Fortunately we can test for weak instruments

Z <- rnorm(10000)
U <- rnorm(10000)
X <- rnorm(10000) + 1*Z + 2*U
Y <- rnorm(10000) + 3*X + 4*U

first_stage <- lm(X~Z)
F <- linearHypothesis(first_stage,"Z=0")$F[2]
F
## [1] 1864.421
  • For a valid instrument, want an F-stat of at least 10
    • Roughly translates to \(T>3.2\)
  • Really, we probably want bigger than this
  • You will learn all about this in PS5

Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

  • So far, an unstated assumption has been that everyone has the same treatment effect:

\(y_i^1-y_i^0 = \delta\) for all \(i\)

  • Of course, this isn’t always true
  • In fact, it’s almost never true
  • This introduces a tradeoff between the internal validity of a study and the external validity
  • Also changes our interpretation of the parameter
  • It also means we need to make three additional assumptions

Assumption 1 - SUTVA

  • SUTVA - Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption
    • Potential outcomes for each person are unrelated to treatment status of others
    • Spillovers are an example
  • Example - looking at the effect of Walmart openings on employment
    • Can’t include neighboring towns because they are partially treated

Assumption 2 - Independence

  • States that assignment of the instrument must be ‘as good as random’
  • Must be unrelated to potential outcomes or potential treatment
  • If IV targets those who benefit most, we have a problem

Assumption 3 - Monotonicity

  • Sounds complicated but is actually straightforward
  • Monotonicity says “the IV (weakly) operates in the same direction on all units”
  • Some people can be unaffected
  • Everyone who is affected must be pushed in the same direction.

Explaining monotonicity

  • Using PO notation once again
  • Each unit starts by getting a value of \(Z\) (0 or 1)
  • Then, they get a value of \(D\) (also 0 or 1)
  • \(D_1 = 0\) means they got a 1 for \(Z\) but a 0 for \(D\)
  • This is like someone having two girls but then deciding they are done This would not violate monotonicity

Monotonicity cont’d

  • Monotonicity essentially says “no defiers”

  • A defier would stop having kids after 2 girls (or 2 boys), but would keep having kids if they had one of each

We never see \(D_{0i}\) and \(D_{1i}\)

But we observe D and Z:

  • If there were defiers, it would change our estimate of the effect of D
  • We need to assume there aren’t any

LATE for class

  • Heterogeneous treatment effects changes our interpretation
  • We no longer estimate an ATE, or even a TOT
  • Now we estimate a LATE
    • Local Average Treatment Effect
  • LATE is the effect of the treatment on those whose treatment status is altered by the instrument

Solution

Popular IV Designs

  • There are many IV designs that have been used repeatedly
  • We will go through 3 of them
    • Lotteries
    • Judge fixed effects
    • Bartik (shift-share) instruments

Lotteries

  • There are often policy ‘treatments’ that many people want
  • When \(Supply < Demand\), spots can be allocated via lotteries
    • Can compare those who signed up and lost with those who won
  • Examples
    • Medicaid experiment (Oregon)
    • School choice lotteries
    • Recent trend - using effectiveness of IVF as a ‘lottery’

Effect of Health Insurance

  • The effect of insurance on health outcomes is not immediately obvious
  • Insurance could lead to overutilization
  • Also potential for a Peltzman Effect
  • In the US, who has insurance is far from random

Enter the Oregon Medicaid Experiment

  • In the early 2000s, Oregon expanded Medicaid
  • Anyone 19-64 under the FPL was eligible to apply
  • Widely advertised and easy to sign up
  • 85k people applied
  • Oregon chose 30k via lottery
  • of them, 10k enrolled

Several influential papers written on oregon experiment

  • Finkelstein et al (2012)
    • \(\uparrow\) utilization
    • \(\downarrow\) out of pocket expenses
    • \(\uparrow\) self-reported physical and mental health
    • No effect on mortality
  • Baicker et al (2012)
    • \(\uparrow\) diagnosis of diabetes and med use
    • \(\downarrow\) probability of depression diagnosis
    • \(\uparrow\) preventive services
    • \(\downarrow\) catastrophic medical expenses

School choice lotteries

  • Mixed results on student achievement

  • Cullen et al (2006) - winning lottery leads to

    • \(\downarrow\) disciplinary events
    • \(\downarrow\) arrests

  • Bibler and Billings (2020) - Losing a school choice lottery leads to residential sorting

  • Bibler et al (2023) - SCL increases arrests for students left behind

IVF as a lottery

  • Understanding the effect of children on labor market outcomes is famously difficult
  • Need a setting where people are similar on observables, but some are randomly allocated children
  • IVF provides this
  • Odds of conceiving are about 40% for 35 years olds, with odds decreasing in age
  • Strategy: compare IVF successes and failures
    • Deals with most of the endogeneity

Lundborg et al (2017)

  • Look at the effect of IVF on women’s careers
  • When IVF is successful
    • \(\downarrow\) hourly earnings
    • \(\downarrow\) employment
    • Effects are long-lasting

Judge Fixed Effects Design

  • We like to think that judges are impartial and fair to all defendants
  • Turns out there are lots of things that can influence judge decisions
    • Lunchtime (Danziger and Levav (2011))
    • College football (Mocan and Eren (2017))
  • It also turns out that some judges are much harsher in general than others

Say we want to know the effect incarceration

  • Typically, you only go to prison for more serious crimes
  • We would expect people sent to prison to have worse outcomes
  • What if two people comitted the same crime, but one gets incarcerated just because they had a harsh judge?
  • Turns out this happens a lot

First used in Gaudet et al (1933)

  • Analyzed 7,000 cases randomly assigned to 6 judges
  • Some judges were almost twice as likely to incarcerate

Judge FE greatest hits

  • Mueller-Smith (2015) - Incarceration leads to

    • \(\uparrow\) recidivism
    • \(\downarrow\) labor market outcomes
    • \(\uparrow\) public assistance

  • Arnold et al (2018) use judge FE’s to show that judges are racially biased against black defendants in bail decision

  • Aizer and Doyle (2015) - being sent to foster care:

    • \(\uparrow\) juvenile delinquency
    • \(\uparrow\) teen pregnancy
    • \(\downarrow\) adult employment

Threats to identification

  • What if a defendant/lawyer knows a judge is harsh
  • If they can get reassigned, then we have a problem
  • Need to know institutional details
  • Still, original assignment could serve as IV

Threats pt 2 - Monotonicity

  • Monotonicity assumption requires judge harshness always work in the same direction
  • If one judge is harsher, they need to be at least as harsh on all cases
  • What if a judge is lenient, but kinda racist?
  • What if a judge is only harsh on drug cases?
  • These are problems, but are testable in the end.

Bartik (shift-share) instruments

  • Say we want to know the effect of employment growth on labor market outcomes
  • OLS is likely hopelessly biased
  • Bartik IVs typically rely on two facts:
    • Employment shocks typically hit different industries
    • Different regions have different industry composition
  • Certain regions are then differentially impacted by national recessions
    • Example - Detroit in 2008-09

Immigration version of Bartik

  • To study the effect of immigration on local labor markets
  • People obviously try to immigrate to places with strong economies
  • There are often ‘push factors’ that cause immigrants to leave a certain area
  • Immigrants typically move to areas where other people from their home country have already moved

Immigration example

  • Early 1900’s - many Norwegians came to the US to flee poverty and religious persecution
  • Different parts of the US will have different ‘stocks’ of those types of immigrants
  • Being in a county with a Norwegian population pre-1900 can then serve as an IV for receiving immigrants

Bartik setup

  • The typically Bartik instrument looks like:

\(B_{l,t} = \sum_{k=1}^K Z_{l,k,t^0}*M_{k,t}\)

  • \(Z_{l,k,t^0}\) is the initial (\(t^0\)) share
    • of county \(l\)
    • from country \(k\) (Norway) to location \(l\)
  • \(M_{k,t}\) is the nationwide change in immigration
    • from country \(k\) at time \(t\) -\(B_{l,t}\) can then measure the effect of immigration on…

Class example - COVID recession shift-share

  • Use county_ind_comp_2019 and covid_emp_industry

  • Calculate the percentage of job loss in each industry using covid_emp_industry. Call this ind_loss

  • Calculate the share of each county’s 2019 employment in each industry (ind_exposure)

  • Merge the two based on naics code

  • Create a county-level measure of exposure to the COVID recession by multiplying ind_loss and ind_exposure

  • Create a county-level map of this measure for the whole US

Tips

  • Use group_by() and then sum() to get total employment in a county
  • When you’ve got your measure, you only want one observation per county
    • Use group_by() then summarise()
  • Also use filter(is.na(covid_exposure)==FALSE)

Solution

covid_emp_industry <- haven::read_dta("covid_emp_industry.dta") %>%
  mutate(ind_loss = (emp_2019-emp_2020)/emp_2019)

county_ind_comp_2019 <- haven::read_dta("county_ind_comp_2019.dta") %>%
  group_by(countyfips) %>%
  mutate(total_emp = sum(employment),
         ind_exposure = employment/total_emp,
         fips = countyfips)

covid_bartik <- merge(covid_emp_industry, county_ind_comp_2019) %>%
  mutate(covid_exposure = ind_loss * ind_exposure) %>%
  group_by(fips) %>%
  summarise(covid_exposure = sum(covid_exposure)) %>%
  filter(is.na(covid_exposure)==FALSE)

Solution

That doesn’t look great. Let’s look at the density

plot(density(covid_bartik$covid_exposure))

covid_bartik <- covid_bartik %>%
  mutate(exp_trunc = ifelse(covid_exposure>.1,.1,covid_exposure))
  • Let’s truncate at .1

Truncated version
